name: Kevin Warsh
role: Chair of the U.S. Federal Reserve (since May 2026); Fed Governor (2006-2011)
summary: A Republican-aligned economist and former Fed Governor who favors an independent central bank focused on price stability, a much smaller Fed balance sheet, and reform of Fed communications and its inflation framework. He criticises large government spending and protectionism, and supports market discipline and lighter regulation. His public record is concentrated on monetary, fiscal and financial policy, with little stated on social or foreign issues.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: In 2025 he called his critique of the Fed a love letter, said that if it reforms the central bank can have another great hundred years, and called for a smaller balance sheet and reform of its role, not its abolition; he then took the Chair (2026).

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: In 2010 said stimulus programs did little to put the economy on a sustainable path, that excessive growth in government spending is "a principal foe", and that fiscal consolidation is preferable; in 2025 criticised Congress for reckless spending in peacetime.

capital-controls.rationale: Listed ad hoc capital controls and unilateral currency measures abroad among distortions and protectionist responses that raise tensions (2010). Not a general statement about state control of capital.

central-bank-independence.rationale: In 2010 called independence in the conduct of monetary policy the cornerstone of the Fed's credibility (while saying it is independence within government, set by Congress); in 2025-26 as Chairman repeated that monetary policy is independent in its conduct, separate from the fiscal authorities.

free-trade.rationale: In 2010 urged policymakers to defend the post-war bipartisan consensus for free trade and the merits of open, competitive markets, and called protectionism "anathema" to pro-growth policy. Did not say it benefits everyone.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In 2010 he said market forces are often more certain than promised fiscal spending multipliers and urged regulators to let firms succeed or fail, hostile to incumbents' rent-seeking.

no-bailouts.rationale: In 2010 said a system is needed in which insolvent firms fail and governments credibly commit to let them fail, calling too-big-to-fail moral hazard unacceptable. But as a Governor he took part in the 2008 rescues, and he supported the 2008 balance-sheet expansion, so the record is mixed.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Criticised implicit government guarantees to large financial firms that create institutions operating under different rules (2010). Concerns financial firms only.

no-central-bank.rationale: In 2025 he said the Fed can have another great hundred years if it reforms itself, and the central bank's job in a panic is to provide liquidity; he argues for narrowing the Fed's role, not for having no central bank.

regulate-corporations.rationale: In 2025 described a "regulatory tax" that has harmed US growth and welcomed its removal; in 2010 doubted that broad new regulatory powers alone would fix finance, preferring market discipline. Does not support tighter regulation of corporations generally.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Called protectionism a "false promise" and its creep anathema to growth (2010). No clear recent statement on tariffs found, so the older position is used.

notes: Second pass (rules 7). Fed Governor speeches of 2010 (monetary independence, regulation, fiscal and trade policy), the April 2025 G30 lecture, the May 2025 Hoover interview and Chairman remarks of June to August 2026 were read in full. Searched for stated positions on trade, tariffs, regulation, fiscal policy, central bank independence, balance sheet, money, taxes and technology. His record is almost wholly monetary, fiscal and financial; no stated position was found on social, cultural, liberty, government-structure or foreign-policy statements, so those are null. Tariff comments in 2025 and 2026 are reported only in news summaries and are not used. The previous Wikipedia citation on abolish-central-banks was replaced by his own words. Fails the uncertainty rule: the record is too narrow.
